pattern: insanity is doing the same thing over and over
likely_origin: 1981 Narcotics Anonymous approval-draft pamphlet (per Quote Investigator)
note: No Einstein source exists; the earliest documented appearance is a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous text. It was widely reassigned to Einstein in the 1980s and 1990s.

pattern: if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree
likely_origin: unknown; no Einstein source, earliest sightings are late twentieth century
note: Wikiquote lists this under Einstein's misattributed section. No source in his writings, letters or interviews has ever been produced.

pattern: compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world
likely_origin: advertising copy of the 1920s-1980s; no Einstein source
note: A staple of financial marketing, attached to Einstein's name without any documented source.

pattern: if you cant explain it simply you dont understand it well enough
likely_origin: unattributed teaching maxim; no Einstein source
note: Listed among Einstein's misattributed quotations; no primary source has been found.

pattern: two things are infinite the universe and human stupidity
likely_origin: attributed to Einstein only in later retellings; earlier forms appear in other writers
note: Frequently attributed to Einstein but unsourced; Wikiquote treats it as unverified.

pattern: not everything that counts can be counted
likely_origin: William Bruce Cameron, Informal Sociology (1963)
note: The line comes from a sociology textbook by William Bruce Cameron, not from Einstein.

pattern: be the change you wish to see in the world
likely_origin: a paraphrase of an 1913 passage in Gandhi's Indian Opinion; not verbatim Gandhi
note: Gandhi wrote something adjacent in 1913, but this compact slogan is a later paraphrase and is not found in his collected works.

pattern: an eye for an eye makes the whole world blind
likely_origin: attributed to Gandhi by later writers; no source in his collected works
note: Widely quoted but never located in Gandhi's writings; Wikiquote lists it as disputed or misattributed.

pattern: first they ignore you then they laugh at you
likely_origin: Nicholas Klein, address to the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America (1918)
note: The structure comes from a 1918 trade-union speech by Nicholas Klein; there is no Gandhi source.

pattern: a lie can travel halfway around the world
likely_origin: lineage runs back to Jonathan Swift (1710) via several nineteenth-century restatements
note: No Twain source exists. Versions of the sentiment predate him by more than a century.

pattern: the coldest winter i ever spent was a summer in san francisco
likely_origin: unknown; not in any Twain text
note: A durable San Francisco joke pinned on Twain with no documented source.

pattern: everybody talks about the weather but nobody does anything about it
likely_origin: Charles Dudley Warner, editorial in the Hartford Courant (1897)
note: Twain's friend and co-author Charles Dudley Warner wrote it; Twain quoted it.

pattern: golf is a good walk spoiled
likely_origin: anonymous nineteenth-century joke; attributed to Twain only after his death
note: No Twain source; the attribution appears decades after the phrase itself.

pattern: lies damned lies and statistics
likely_origin: Twain credited Disraeli, but the attribution to Disraeli is itself unverified
note: Twain popularised the phrase while crediting Benjamin Disraeli; no Disraeli source has been found, so the true origin remains open.

pattern: if youre going through hell keep going
likely_origin: unknown; attributed to Churchill only from the late twentieth century
note: Not found in Churchill's speeches or writings; the Churchill Centre lists it among quotations he never said.

pattern: success is not final failure is not fatal
likely_origin: unknown; circulating in American motivational literature before being attached to Churchill
note: No Churchill source. Wikiquote lists it under misattributed.

pattern: the best argument against democracy is a five minute conversation
likely_origin: unknown; no Churchill source
note: A popular but unsourced line; the Churchill archives have never located it.

pattern: success is stumbling from failure to failure with no loss of enthusiasm
likely_origin: unknown; attached to Churchill in twentieth-century motivational collections
note: No Churchill source; listed among the quotations most often wrongly attributed to him.

pattern: i disapprove of what you say but i will defend to the death your right to say it
likely_origin: Evelyn Beatrice Hall, The Friends of Voltaire (1906), summarising his attitude
note: Hall wrote the sentence as a summary of Voltaire's position; it was later quoted as though it were his.

pattern: with great power comes great responsibility
likely_origin: French National Convention decree (1793); popularised by Spider-Man comics
note: Attributed to Voltaire online with no source; the closest documented antecedent is a 1793 French National Convention text.

pattern: you can fool all the people some of the time
likely_origin: attributed to Lincoln from the 1880s; no contemporaneous record
note: No verified Lincoln source; the earliest attributions appear two decades after his death.

pattern: whatever you are be a good one
likely_origin: unknown; first attributed to Lincoln in the twentieth century
note: No Lincoln source has ever been produced for this line.

pattern: let them eat cake
likely_origin: Rousseau's Confessions (written 1765), attributed to an unnamed great princess
note: Rousseau records the remark years before Marie Antoinette arrived in France; the attribution to her is revolutionary-era propaganda.

pattern: the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing
likely_origin: unknown; no such sentence in Burke's works
note: Burke wrote something loosely related about the association of good men, but this famous form is not his.

pattern: boldness has genius power and magic in it
likely_origin: W. H. Murray's The Scottish Himalayan Expedition (1951), quoting a loose translation
note: Murray printed these lines as a couplet after his own paragraph on commitment; they are not a faithful Goethe translation.

pattern: what lies behind us and what lies before us are tiny matters
likely_origin: Henry Stanley Haskins, Meditations in Wall Street (1940)
note: The passage comes from Haskins's anonymous 1940 book, not from Emerson.

pattern: do not go where the path may lead
likely_origin: Muriel Strode, Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers (1903)
note: Strode wrote the original first-person line; the imperative Emerson version is a later rewrite.

pattern: to be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else
likely_origin: unknown; also widely misattributed to E. E. Cummings
note: No Emerson source; the line circulates under several famous names with none verified.

pattern: we are what we repeatedly do
likely_origin: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), summarising Aristotle
note: Durant's summary of the Nicomachean Ethics, not a translation of Aristotle's own words.

pattern: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts
likely_origin: a loose rendering of a passage in the Metaphysics; the slogan form is twentieth-century Gestalt psychology
note: Aristotle says something narrower about wholes and parts; the familiar slogan is a modern compression.

pattern: only the dead have seen the end of war
likely_origin: George Santayana, Soliloquies in England (1922)
note: Santayana wrote it; the attribution to Plato spread through a twentieth-century misquotation.

pattern: choose a job you love and you will never have to work
likely_origin: unknown; earliest sightings are twentieth-century American career advice
note: Nothing in the Analects corresponds to this; the Confucius attribution is modern.

pattern: holding on to anger is like grasping a hot coal
likely_origin: a modern paraphrase; the closest canonical text differs substantially
note: Popular in Western collections; not a translation of any single Pali canon passage.

pattern: history is written by the victors
likely_origin: unknown; no primary source under any of the usual names
note: Attributed variously to Churchill and Napoleon; no documented source exists for either.

pattern: beer is proof that god loves us
likely_origin: a garbled version of Franklin's 1779 letter about wine and rain
note: Franklin wrote about wine, not beer, and made a different point entirely.

pattern: the price of freedom is eternal vigilance
likely_origin: John Philpot Curran (1790), later popularised by Wendell Phillips
note: The Jefferson Monticello project lists this among quotations he never wrote.

pattern: a government big enough to give you everything you want
likely_origin: Gerald R. Ford, address to Congress (1974), itself echoing earlier phrasings
note: Not found in Jefferson's papers; the earliest close match is twentieth-century.

pattern: it is not the strongest of the species that survives
likely_origin: Leon C. Megginson, paraphrasing Darwin in a 1963 lecture
note: A management-school paraphrase that hardened into a Darwin quotation.

pattern: the ends justify the means
likely_origin: a compression of a qualified passage in The Prince; the slogan is not his sentence
note: Machiavelli's actual passage is narrower and conditional; the slogan form is a later invention.

pattern: if i had asked people what they wanted they would have said faster horses
likely_origin: no contemporaneous source; first attributed to Ford decades after his death
note: A staple of product-management folklore with no documented Ford source.

pattern: culture eats strategy for breakfast
likely_origin: attributed to Drucker in consulting literature; absent from his published work
note: No source in Drucker's books or papers has been identified.

pattern: what gets measured gets managed
likely_origin: attributed to Drucker without a located source; similar phrasings predate him
note: Frequently quoted as Drucker's; the sentence has not been found in his writing.

pattern: in a time of universal deceit telling the truth is a revolutionary act
likely_origin: unknown; the Orwell Foundation has found no source in his work
note: Not in Nineteen Eighty-Four or any essay; attributed to Orwell from the 1980s onwards.

pattern: people sleep peaceably in their beds at night only because rough men stand ready
likely_origin: a paraphrase of Richard Grenier's 1993 gloss on an Orwell essay
note: Grenier paraphrased Orwell without quotation marks; the sentence then circulated as Orwell's own.

pattern: luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity
likely_origin: twentieth-century aphorism, often credited to Darrell Royal
note: Seneca wrote about fortune and preparation in different terms; this compact form is modern.

pattern: our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate
likely_origin: Marianne Williamson, A Return to Love (1992)
note: Often said to be from Mandela's 1994 inaugural address; it appears nowhere in that speech.

pattern: we dont see things as they are we see them as we are
likely_origin: an older aphorism of uncertain origin, often traced to the Talmud
note: Nin quoted a version of it; the sentiment substantially predates her.

pattern: those who would give up essential liberty to purchase a little temporary safety
likely_origin: Franklin's 1755 Pennsylvania Assembly letter, routinely quoted out of its original context
note: The words are close to Franklin's, but the passage concerned a tax dispute and is habitually misapplied.

pattern: the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago
likely_origin: unknown; commonly labelled a Chinese proverb with no Chinese source
note: No original text has been identified in any language; the proverb label appears to be modern packaging.
